description: Equipo de CS en Hermosillo explorando datos de radar NISAR (SAR) para detectar cambios en la superficie terrestre.
summary:
Sparks puts NASA's SPHEREx telescope in anyone's hands. Type any sky position, or pick one of the five challenge targets, and in seconds Sparks blinks the SPHEREx images of that field taken months apart, exactly the way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930, now in 102 infrared colors. Anything that moved jumps off the screen: blue shows where it was, amber where it is now, and Sparks draws and measures the arrow between them.

It works. On Barnard's Star, the fastest star in the sky, Sparks measures 10.23″/yr, matching ESA's Gaia (10.39″/yr) to within 0.4σ. It also tracks WISE 0855, the coldest brown dwarf ever found, an object Gaia cannot even see, and reveals its cold infrared fingerprint. With one click you get any point's spectrum across every exposure, Gaia and CatWISE overlays, and a plain-language verdict on what happened, backed by a machine-learning classifier that is right 78% of the time.

SPHEREx photographs the entire sky every six months, far more than any team of astronomers can inspect by hand. Sparks runs in any browser, even on a phone, with no install and no account, turning that flood of data into something students, teachers and citizen scientists can explore. Citizen scientists have already found most known brown dwarfs by comparing images; Sparks gives them SPHEREx to do it again.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sparks is a blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey, running entirely in a web browser.

- Enter coordinates in degrees (269.4486 4.7672), sexagesimal (17:57:48.5 +04:41:36), or choose one of the five challenge targets.

- See the field in all six SPHEREx detectors in three modes: Blink (alternate observing seasons), Sum (average of seasons, lower noise) and Difference (one season minus another, in units of noise sigma). Blue marks where a source was; amber where it is now.

- Measure the proper-motion arrow and compare it with Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020, whose sources can be overlaid on the image.

- Click any point to get its spectrum on the fly, measured across every individual exposure (102 infrared colors, 0.75–5 µm).

- A "What happened?" panel gives a plain-language verdict: moves, changes brightness, or cannot be measured, and why.

- A small machine-learning classifier suggests the object type as a candidate, with its accuracy shown next to it.

- NASA quality flags, per-detector noise and the source of every number are shown. The full view is encoded in the URL, so any view can be shared. English and Spanish.

RESULTS ON THE FIVE CHALLENGE TARGETS

- Barnard's Star: 10.23 ± 0.43″/yr vs. 10.39″/yr in Gaia DR3 (0.4σ).

- WISE 0855−0714: 6.04 ± 0.76″/yr vs. 8.09″/yr in the catalog (2.7σ, flagged for review); at least 10× more light at 4.7 µm (D6) than at 1.35 µm (D2), the signature of a very cold brown dwarf. Not detected by Gaia.

- epsilon Indi B: 4.21 ± 0.28″/yr vs. 4.68″/yr in Gaia DR3, over 4 seasons.

- RW Aurigae: no significant motion; reported as an upper limit, not as motion.

- R Draconis: saturated in all six detectors; Sparks explains why there is no measurement instead of inventing one.

- Object-type classifier (random forest on Gaia luminosity and color): 78.3% leave-one-out accuracy on 69 objects with verified class (majority-class baseline 29.0%, permutation test p = 0.03).

HOW IT WORKS

1. Pipeline (Python): queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx images of each field (DR1, QR2, QR3), cuts 64 × 64 pixel stamps (6.56′ wide, 6.15″/pixel), aligns them, subtracts the zodiacal background, removes neighbor stars, and builds per-detector, per-season stacks and difference images with their noise maps. It then fits the motion across seasons and measures the infrared spectrum.

2. Data package: each field becomes a small set of static files (manifest, catalogs, binary image cubes), 1.8–7.9 MB per field.

3. Web app (React + TypeScript + Vite): reads those files directly, renders the images without altering the raw pixels (overlays go on a separate layer), and computes spectra and field-of-view crops in the browser. It is a static site served from AWS (S3 + CloudFront): adding a patch of sky means adding a file, not a server.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Opens SPHEREx's time-domain data to students, teachers and citizen scientists with no installation and no account, on a laptop or a phone.

- Honest by design: every number shows its source and uncertainty, disagreements are flagged, and the tool never claims discoveries.

- Cheap to scale: static files on a CDN, no backend.

- Next step: run the same pipeline patch by patch over the whole SPHEREx sky so volunteers can review moving and variable candidates, as Backyard Worlds did with WISE, and hand promising candidates to professional astronomers.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Sparks brings back the 1930 blink comparator that found Pluto and applies it to a 102-color infrared survey. A single blue/amber color code, used everywhere, makes motion readable at a glance, and every target gets a plain-language verdict instead of a raw table.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (uncertainties, upper limits, saturated targets explained), accessibility for non-experts, mobile use, bilingual copy, and keeping the raw sky pixels untouched.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, Python (NumPy, Astropy), scikit-learn (classifier), Vitest (unit tests), AWS S3 + CloudFront for hosting, GitHub for version control.

Source code: https://github.com/EL-CONS/SPARKS-PROJECT
